tip: 'Picante' is spicy-hot in flavor; 'quente' is hot in temperature. 'Comida picante' burns the tongue.
'Preferir' doesn't need a preposition – just 'prefiro café' or 'prefiro ir a pé.' Unlike 'gostar de' and 'precisar de.'
'Tempo' means both weather and time; 'está horrível hoje' shows it is the weather here.
'O problema do trânsito': 'do' = 'de' + 'o' (of the, masculine). You'll almost never see 'de o' written out.
'Estão cheias' uses 'estar' because crowded is the streets' condition right now, not a permanent trait; 'ser' would sound inherent.
'Dele/dela' = his/her. More specific than 'seu/sua' which can mean his/her/your.
Verbs ending in '-gar' add a 'u' in the 'eu' past to keep the hard 'g' sound: 'pagar' becomes 'paguei.'
'Foto' is feminine ('a foto') because it's short for 'fotografia.' Similarly, 'moto' is feminine ('a moto') from 'motocicleta.'
In Brazilian Portuguese, 'tem' is commonly used to mean 'there is/there are,' even though formal grammar prefers 'há.'
For where movable things are located, use 'estar': 'os sapatos estão debaixo da cama,' not 'são.'
'Gostar de' + infinitive for activities: 'não gosta de acordar.' The 'de' is always required before the verb.
'Perto de' means near, and the 'de' contracts with the article: 'de' + 'o' = 'do', giving 'perto do trabalho.'
Adjectives ending in '-e' don't change for gender: 'quente' is the same for masculine and feminine. Only number changes: 'quentes.'
'Falar com' = to speak with or to someone: 'falei com o gerente.' Portuguese usually uses 'com' where English says 'to.'
'Emprestar' in Brazilian Portuguese means both 'to lend' and 'to borrow.' Context clarifies: 'emprestei para ele' = I lent to him; 'emprestei dele' = I borrowed from him.
'Férias' is always plural in Portuguese – there's no singular form. 'As férias' = vacation(s).
'Precisar de' = to need (something). Like 'gostar de,' the 'de' is required before a noun: 'preciso de mais tempo.'
'Cor' is feminine: 'a cor.' Some nouns don't follow the '-o/-a' pattern and must be memorized.
For '-ar' verbs the 'nós' form is identical in present and past, so 'jantamos' can mean we dine or we dined, and context decides.
'Vai à academia': 'à' = 'a' + 'a' (to the, feminine) – the famous 'crase', marked with its own accent.
'Problema' is masculine ('o problema') despite ending in '-a.' This is one of the most common gender mistakes learners make.
'Trazer' (to bring) is irregular in the past: 'eu trouxe,' not the expected 'trazi.'
'Gostar' always needs 'de' where English 'like' takes no preposition: it is 'gosta de acordar', and dropping the 'de' breaks it.
'São fartos' uses 'ser' because generous portions are the inherent character of 'mineira' cooking, not a passing state.
'Procurar' means to look for and normally takes a direct object: 'procuramos o restaurante,' with no preposition.
The superlative frame is 'o mais alto da família', where Portuguese says of the family where English says in the family.
'Fazer trilha' means to hike. Brazilians use 'fazer' in many leisure expressions: 'fazer mergulho' (dive), 'fazer escalada' (climb), 'fazer rapel' (rappel).
Unlike Spanish 'gustar', Portuguese 'gostar' keeps normal order: subject plus 'gostam de churrasco', with no subject flip.
Adjectives agree in gender: 'deliciosa' (fem.) matches 'comida' (fem.). Masculine would be 'delicioso.'
'Desculpa' is the casual sorry; 'desculpe' is more formal. Brazilians say 'desculpa' with friends and family.
